title: Sell Mineral Rights in Alpena County, MI
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Alpena County, MI
metaDescription: Alpena County, MI mineral rights owner? Limestone and Traverse Group history, split-estate ownership, honest pricing. Get a real evaluation, no games.
heroLead: Alpena County's economy runs on limestone as much as anything, but the oil and gas history underneath that same ground is real, and if you hold a mineral interest here, it deserves an honest look, not a form-letter offer.
intro: Alpena County, seat at Alpena on Lake Huron, is better known for its cement plants and limestone quarries than for oil and gas, and that's fair, the Alpena limestone formation has driven the local economy for over a century. But mineral ownership in this county isn't limited to limestone rights. Oil and gas leasing and drilling reached Alpena County too, tied to the Traverse Group and Devonian reef and reservoir rock that runs through this part of the Michigan Basin, and plenty of families here hold a mineral interest they've never had properly explained to them.

We evaluate mineral and royalty interests across Alpena County, from the city itself out through Ossineke and the surrounding townships. A lot of what we see is small legacy interests tied to farm and forest land that's changed hands multiple times over the decades, with the mineral estate frequently split off from the surface somewhere along the way.

sections.heading: Not Antrim core, but real oil and gas history
paragraphs: Alpena County sits outside the tight Antrim Shale core of Otsego, Antrim, Kalkaska, and Montmorency counties, which means the drilling pattern here looks different, more scattered, tied to Traverse Group limestone and Devonian reef trends that run through the Michigan Basin rather than dense Antrim spacing. Some sections in the county have real production history behind them, others were leased over the decades without ever being drilled.

That's important context because it means we can't assume an Alpena County interest looks like one from Gaylord or Kalkaska. Each parcel gets checked against its own lease and production history before we say anything about value.

sections.heading: Limestone, quarrying, and mineral estate complexity
paragraphs: Because limestone quarrying has been the dominant extraction industry in Alpena County for so long, some parcels here carry a layered mineral history, surface rights, limestone or aggregate rights, and oil and gas rights that may have been severed from each other at different points over the decades by different owners. That's a more complicated picture than a straightforward oil and gas split estate, and it matters when you're trying to figure out exactly what you own.

If you're not sure whether your family's mineral interest covers oil and gas, limestone, or both, that's worth sorting out before any sale conversation, and it usually starts with pulling the full chain of title.

sections.heading: How ownership typically breaks down here
paragraphs: Most of the mineral ownership we see in Alpena County traces back to farm and homestead land, split off from the surface through a sale, a reservation in a deed, or inheritance that scattered a single original interest across several heirs over generations. The Alpena County register of deeds, located in Alpena, holds the recorded documents that establish that chain, and pulling it is usually the first step toward understanding what you actually hold.

It's common for an owner here to receive a small, irregular royalty payment and have no idea which well, which lease, or which company it's actually tied to. That's fixable with the right records request.

sections.heading: Pricing an Alpena County interest honestly
paragraphs: Where there's active or historical oil and gas production tied to your interest, we check current volumes against your actual royalty statements, along with net mineral acres and the well's remaining production life. Where the interest has only ever been leased without a well, the value proposition is more speculative and tied to future leasing potential rather than an income stream. We'll tell you plainly which category your interest falls into before quoting anything.

faqs.question: Is Alpena County part of the Antrim Shale trend?
faqs.answer: No, it sits outside the tight Antrim core to the west and south. Oil and gas activity here is more tied to Traverse Group and Devonian reef trends, and drilling has historically been more scattered than the dense Antrim spacing seen in counties like Otsego or Kalkaska.

faqs.question: My deed mentions limestone rights, not oil and gas. Do I still own mineral rights?
faqs.answer: It depends on the exact language and the chain of title. Some Alpena County parcels have limestone or aggregate rights and oil and gas rights that were severed separately over the years. Pulling the full recorded chain at the county register of deeds is the way to know for sure.

faqs.question: I get an occasional small royalty check but don't know which well it's from. How do I find out?
faqs.answer: Contact the operator listed on your check or statement and ask for a copy of your division order, which identifies the specific well and your decimal interest in it. We can help you work through that if you send us what you have.

faqs.question: Is a mineral interest that's only been leased, never drilled, worth anything in Alpena County?
faqs.answer: It can have some speculative value tied to future leasing potential, but it's a different situation from a producing royalty interest with actual income history. We'll be upfront about which category yours falls into.

faqs.question: What paperwork should I gather before contacting you about Alpena County minerals?
faqs.answer: Your deed or probate document, any royalty statements or division orders you've received, and if available, the legal description or section-township-range for your interest. Partial records are still a useful starting point.
